https://www.politico.eu/article/france-c.text: PARIS — The French government will need to green light attempts by non-European investors to acquire more than 10 percent of shares in French companies “operating in a sensitive sector” and listed on a stock market outside the EU, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said. “Against a backdrop of heightened geopolitical tensions, we are strengthening oversight of foreign investments in sensitive sectors,” the French leader wrote on X on Sunday. “Our responsibility is twofold: to support the growth of French businesses while safeguarding our strategic interests.” The threshold will apply to government-designated sectors including defense, critical infrastructure and key technologies. Advertisement Advertisement Earlier this year, Lecornu asked three parliamentarians from his center-right coalition to report on France’s economic security. Obtained by POLITICO , the document called for a “radical change in posture” and urged the government to take “a holistic approach” to protecting strategic assets, securing critical supply chains, reducing dependencies and strengthening technological sovereignty. In a press release on the threshold change, Lecornu’s office said the government would give its response on any proposed foreign investments within 10 days of notification to “avoid placing an undue burden on companies’ ability to raise capital in financial markets.” The move is intended to “guard against opportunistic acquisitions by non-EU investors in French companies listed outside the EU that could pose risks to national security,” the statement noted. France had previously set up a screening process for planned acquisitions of over 10 percent of shares in French companies listed on European markets during Covid-19, with the stated aim of “protecting strategic companies” in a time of crisis. The measure was later made permanent and is now being extended to French companies listed outside the EU. The new rules will come into effect in the coming days. Other EU countries, such as Germany and Spain , have similar foreign investment screening regimes that apply a 10 percent threshold to acquisitions in certain strategic sectors. Paul de Villepin contributed to this report. Advertisement Advertisement

Photograph: PR Add to playlist Music The week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: Dutch squat-punks Bombstrap’s uncompromising racket The Rotterdam band are a riot of sound, look and attitude led by Eva Kah, who is as much a living artwork as she is a phenomenal live performer Richard Foster Fri 30 Oct 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 08.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google From Rotterdam, the Netherlands Recommended if you like Gnod, Discharge, Gwar Up next Debut album Big Enemy out now via Tartarus, playing Le Guess Who festival Rotterdam’s Bombstrap are a riotous and theatrical fusion of sound, look and attitude. An embodied version of John Milton’s Pandæmonium with the amp turned up to 11, the band revel in hardcore alternative living, internet wormholes, art-school pretensions and a gungy form of hardcore. Based in and drawing succour from one of the most famous squatted centres in the city, Het Poortgebouw, Bombstrap are a noisy counterblast to the increasing and overwhelmingly witless “circuses-and-bread” gentrification of Rotterdam. Visual artist and singer Eva Kah is a living artwork and phenomenal live performer, whose in-your-face act illuminates those grey areas between righteous anger, nihilistic energy and teeth-grating bad taste. Kah’s vocals ape the warning screams and ululations a crone would make over the grave of Achilles. A natural extension of the look, obviously. Some of the uncompromising attitudes heard in debut album Big Enemy also betray their links to Manchester’s punk and squat scenes; previous members of the extended Gnod family have played with them. But the sound is a shifting, amorphous one, permanently up for grabs in the listener’s interpretation. The gravelly mix of chopped-up rhythms and raw, high-decibel punk guitars could even hark back to ancient prog-punk gonzoids such as the Pink Fairies. They are one of the last cries of homegrown, communal, anarcho hippy-punkdom and have all the social and sonic baggage that that entails. There is no career path in sight. Richard Foster This week’s best new tracks View image in fullscreen Deep and dramatic … Clementine Douglas. Photograph: Lily Ajaib Clementine Douglas​ – So Precious Self-penned, and gorgeously self-produced with a ribbon of synth melody pirouetting from the bottom of the mix, this is deep and dramatic vocal house from the British singer normally found belting alongside Calvin Harris, Dom Dolla et al. ​DJ Heartstring – 3am/4am (ft Monk, 3ndles5 & Crazymike) The German dance duo get their countryman Monk to flow over their breakbeat euphoria, while there are shades of Real Lies’ nocturnal social realism to 3ndles5’s spoken English-language verse. Josh Johnson – Jazz Chord Possession Jazz saxophonist Johnson is sideman to Jeff Parker and producer to Meshell Ndegeocello and Flea. His own latest single has two sweetly swaying melodic motifs set against each other, plus analogue synth burbling out back. ​Isaac Kniveton​ – Love Groove Like a colourful plastic playground with its edges melting in the sun, there’s a bright psychedelia to the way the British producer’s Kompakt-style techno-pop unfolds, peppy and woozy all at once. Anamanaguchi – Sucker Punch The New Yorkers pair crunching, muscular chords with delicate electronic detailing, building up a dense bank of shoegaze that’s illuminated from within by a thousand points of neon light. ​Metoronori – Lights of the Bay Dreampop is an overused phrase, but it’s appropriate for the otherworldly beauty and wrongfooting shifts in the Japanese singer-producer’s new album, Forgot Reef Number: this track has a music-box prettiness. Waterbaby – Creek We loved her album Memory Be a Blade earlier this year, and the Stockholm singer-songwriter is back with this waltzing lullaby, full of her trademark blend of wounded emotion and stoic endurance.
